cards.title: The tunnel to nowhere
cards.text: A miner named William "Burro" Schmidt dug a tunnel through the El Paso Mountains with a pick, a shovel, a four-pound hammer, and carefully placed dynamite. He began in 1906, and by 1938 he had reached his goal. Schmidt said he would never haul his ore to the Mojave smelter down the back trail with his two burros. A road from Last Chance Canyon to Mojave was completed in 1920, but he kept digging. He never used the tunnel to carry ore.

cards.title: A landing field becomes a weapons laboratory
cards.text: China Lake began as an emergency landing field that the Works Progress Administration built in the early 1930s near the town of Inyokern. The field opened in 1935, and the Army Air Forces acquired it in 1942. In November 1943, it was transferred to the Navy, which made it the Naval Ordnance Test Station. The desert around it is vast and sparsely populated, with near-perfect flying weather and practically unlimited visibility.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: Bigger than Rhode Island
cards.text: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake covers more than 1.1 million acres, an area larger than the state of Rhode Island. It is the Navy's largest single landholding. The part of the base inside Kern County is about 1.4 percent of the county, as of 2024.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: Five inches of rain
cards.text: At China Lake, in eastern Kern County, only about 4.7 inches of rain falls in an average year. The average temperature over the year is about 65 degrees. July afternoons average a high near 105 degrees. January nights average a low of about 31 degrees.

cards.title: What the county government does with its money
cards.text: Kern County's government spent about 2.6 billion dollars in 2022. It had about 10,000 full-time employees that year. Property taxes brought in about 423 million dollars of its tax revenue. An elected board of five supervisors, serving four-year terms, governs the county.

cards.title: A base of 470 square miles
cards.text: Edwards Air Force Base covers 301,000 acres, about 470 square miles. More than 120 million dollars was spent to develop and expand it in the 1940s. About 4 percent of Kern County lies inside the base, as of 2024.

cards.title: Breaking the sound barrier
cards.text: On October 14, 1947, over what is now Edwards Air Force Base, Captain Chuck Yeager became the first person to fly faster than the speed of sound. He flew a Bell XS-1 nicknamed Glamorous Glennis, and a sonic boom was heard across the Mojave Desert. The flight was over Rogers Dry Lake, a dry lakebed so flat that it could serve as a giant runway. Back then the base was called Muroc, a reversal of Corum, because California already had a town named Coram. It was later renamed for Captain Glen Edwards, who died in 1948 in the crash of a Northrop YB-49 flying wing.

cards.title: A mining town was the first county seat
cards.text: Kern County's first county seat was Havilah, a mining town, not Bakersfield. The county was created in 1866 from southern Tulare County, with added land from Los Angeles and San Bernardino Counties. The seat moved to Bakersfield in 1874.

cards.title: Pistachios in a dry valley
cards.text: A company that grows pistachios in the Indian Wells Valley went to court over a fee for pumping the valley's groundwater. The local groundwater authority set a replenishment fee of 2,130 dollars an acre-foot, starting in January 2021. The grower, Mojave Pistachios, argued the fee infringed on its water rights. In February 2024, the California Court of Appeals ruled in the authority's favor.

cards.title: One basin, no backup
cards.text: The towns around Ridgecrest and the China Lake base draw their water from one underground basin, with no significant surface water or imported supply. The state has determined that the Indian Wells Valley groundwater basin is in critical overdraft, from decades of over-pumping. The basin spans about 600 square miles across parts of Kern, Inyo, and San Bernardino Counties. Groundwater levels there have been declining since 1945. State law requires pumping and recharge to be brought into balance by 2040.

cards.title: Two towns moved for the lake
cards.text: To make room for the Isabella Dam reservoir, the towns of Lake Isabella and Kernville both had to be moved to higher ground. Most of the original town of Kernville had been razed in 1948. Construction began in 1948 and finished in March 1953. Lake Isabella can hold up to 570,000 acre-feet of water, with a surface area of 11,200 acres.

cards.title: Raising a dam sixteen feet
cards.text: The Army Corps of Engineers raised both the main and auxiliary dams at Lake Isabella by 16 feet. A seepage problem was found in the auxiliary dam on April 28, 2006, and the lake was held 20 feet below its normal full level. The work also added a new 28-foot-high labyrinth weir, and it targeted three failure risks: overtopping, seepage, and earthquake damage. The safety improvements were substantially completed in November 2022.

cards.title: The Kawaiisu homeland
cards.text: The Kawaiisu live in the Tehachapi Valley and north across Tehachapi Pass, toward Lake Isabella and Walker Pass. They call themselves Nüwa, which means the People. Before European contact, they lived in permanent winter villages of 60 to 100 people. They also traveled east on food-gathering trips into the northern Mojave Desert, as far as the Panamint Valley. The Kawaiisu once made their home around what is now Red Rock Canyon State Park, and they left petroglyphs in the El Paso Mountains.

cards.title: Oil at seventy feet
cards.text: In 1899, Tom Means persuaded Frank Wiseman and others to dig for oil in what became the Kern River Oil Field, and they found it at 70 feet. Kern County's economy is still heavily linked to agriculture and petroleum extraction.

cards.title: A preserve on an old cattle ranch
cards.text: The Kern River Preserve, near Weldon, is owned by the National Audubon Society. It covers about 3,000 acres on the former cattle ranch of Andrew Brown, which dates to the 1860s. The preserve was established in 1979. The South Fork Kern River, which flows through it into Lake Isabella, has been a national Wild and Scenic River since 1987. The preserve protects habitat for the federally listed endangered southwestern willow flycatcher.

cards.title: Who owns the land
cards.text: Government agencies and conservation groups manage about a third of Kern County, as of 2024. The Bureau of Land Management has the biggest share, about 14 percent of the county, and its Ridgecrest Field Office alone covers nearly 10 percent. The Forest Service manages about 7 percent, most of it Sequoia National Forest. The Defense Department holds about 5.5 percent, nearly all of it Edwards Air Force Base and China Lake.

cards.title: From county airfield to airliner parking lot
cards.text: Kern County opened the Mojave Airport in 1935. After the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, the Marine Corps took it over and expanded it into a Marine Corps Auxiliary Air Station. Today the airport is also known as a place where commercial airliners are stored, because of the vast area and dry desert conditions.

cards.title: Where the twenty-mule teams stopped
cards.text: Mojave was the western end of the twenty-mule-team borax route from Death Valley. In the 1880s, teams hauled borax about 165 miles from Death Valley to the railroad at Mojave. The town began in 1876 as a construction camp on the Southern Pacific Railroad. It later served as headquarters for construction of the Los Angeles Aqueduct.

cards.title: The first private spaceflight
cards.text: Mojave Air and Space Port was the base of the first privately funded human spaceflight, SpaceShipOne's flight on June 21, 2004. SpaceShipOne went on to win the X Prize with flights on September 29 and October 4, 2004.

cards.title: A county named for a mapmaker
cards.text: Kern County is named for the Kern River, and the river is named for a mapmaker. Edward Kern was the cartographer on John Frémont's 1845 expedition, which crossed Walker Pass. In 1776, a Spanish priest, Father Francisco Garcés, had called the same river the Rio Bravo de San Felipe.

cards.title: Who lives here
cards.text: About 915,000 people live in Kern County, as of 2024, spread across about 8,135 square miles of land. Half of its residents are younger than about 33. The median household income was about 70,200 dollars a year. The median home was worth about 338,000 dollars.

cards.title: A gold camp that grew up overnight
cards.text: In April 1895, Frederic Mooers, John Singleton, and Charles Burcham found gold at the Yellow Aster Mine, and a camp that became Randsburg grew around it. The mine and camp were named for the Rand, the gold mining region of South Africa. By the end of 1896, more than 1,500 people lived in the camp. As of 2020, Randsburg had 45 residents.

cards.title: Cliffs striped red and white
cards.text: The cliffs of Red Rock Canyon State Park get their vivid colors from alternating layers of white clay and red sandstone. The park covers about 27,000 acres along Highway 14, about 25 miles northeast of Mojave. In the early 1870s, its colorful formations served as landmarks for twenty-mule-team freight wagons. The area was once home to the Kawaiisu people. The state park was created in 1968.

cards.title: A desert backlot
cards.text: Movies shot at Red Rock Canyon State Park include Jurassic Park, Beneath the Planet of the Apes, and Westworld. Television series filmed there include Airwolf and Lost in Space.

cards.title: The Ridgecrest earthquakes
cards.text: The 2019 Ridgecrest earthquakes began with a magnitude 6.4 shock on July 4 and a magnitude 7.1 the next evening. More than 1,400 earthquakes were recorded by the evening of July 5, and more than 3,000 by the morning of July 7. The shaking was felt as far north as Sacramento, as far east as Phoenix, and as far south as Baja California. One person died and 25 were injured.

cards.title: The base that stopped
cards.text: After the July 2019 earthquakes, China Lake evacuated all nonessential personnel and was declared not mission capable. Aerial photographs showed a lateral offset of three to five feet on a service road. The Navy's damage assessment totaled about 5.2 billion dollars. Replacing the buildings alone would cost about 2.2 billion dollars.

cards.title: A missile from the Mojave
cards.text: The Sidewinder air-to-air missile came out of China Lake, then called the Naval Ordnance Test Station. Scientists and engineers there developed the AIM-9 version of the Sidewinder in 1950. William McLean led the project team developing it from 1945 to 1954. Its variants and upgrades are still in active service.

near.name: Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake

cards.title: People of the upper Kern River
cards.text: The Tübatulabal are an Indigenous people of the upper Kern River valley, in the southern Sierra Nevada. Their name loosely translates as pine-nut eaters, from a word for people who go to the forest to gather piñon nuts. Acorns and piñon nuts were staples of their diet, with fish second in importance. They had three bands, the Pahkanapil, the Palegawan, and the Bankalachi, and spoke mutually intelligible dialects of a Uto-Aztecan language. A Tübatulabal tribe, with an office in Mountain Mesa, has been seeking federal recognition.

cards.title: Around the world without stopping
cards.text: The Rutan Voyager, the first aircraft to fly around the world nonstop and unrefueled, was built in Mojave. Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew it in December 1986.

cards.title: A pass that has barely changed
cards.text: Apart from the paved road, Walker Pass is essentially unaltered since Joseph R. Walker mapped it in 1834. John Frémont's survey expedition used the pass in 1845, and Frémont suggested it be named for Walker. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses there.

cards.title: A city planned for the desert
cards.text: California City dates to 1958, when developers bought 82,000 acres of desert to build a metropolis. The plan came from Nat Mendelsohn, a real estate developer and sociology professor, who wanted a community that would join the ranks of America's great cities. Streets were named after top universities and car makers, such as Stanford, Yale, Pontiac, and Cadillac. Vacant lots sold for 990 dollars. By 1962, only 175 homes had been built, and the grid of paved roads still has little construction.

cards.title: The third-largest city by area
cards.text: California City covers about 204 square miles, the third-largest land area of any city in California, behind San Diego and Los Angeles. Its plan included a central park with a 26-acre manmade lake and two golf courses. When it incorporated in 1965, it had 5,900 landowners but only 817 residents.

cards.title: From freeway to expressway
cards.text: Between 1963 and 1975, significant portions of US 6, now Highway 14, were moved to a freeway alignment. The last interchange near California City is California City Boulevard, and the road's character changes there. The former routing south of Mojave and the current routing to the north are both still known as Sierra Highway.

cards.title: The Fremont Valley
cards.text: The Fremont Valley stretches from the town of Mojave about 70 kilometers northeast to the foothills of the Lava Mountains and Summit Range. The Rand Mountains lie at its eastern edge, the southern Sierra Nevada form its western border, and the Tehachapi Mountains border it from the southwest. Koehn Dry Lake lies in the valley, along with the communities of California City and Cantil.

cards.title: The wilderness of the El Paso Mountains
cards.text: The El Paso Mountains Wilderness covers about 23,780 acres and was created in 1994. Its central feature is Black Mountain, an extinct volcano and the highest point in the range. Wildlife there includes raptors, the Mohave ground squirrel, and the desert tortoise. Joshua trees grow on the western side of the mountain.

cards.title: Last Chance Canyon
cards.text: Last Chance Canyon runs through the El Paso Mountains from Saltdale in the south to Black Mountain in the north. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on December 5, 1972, and is known as the Last Chance Archaeological District. The canyon includes pictographs, villages, rock shelters, mills, and quarries, along with gold mining camps. The canyon is open to hiking, camping, and four-wheel-drive vehicles in most parts.

cards.title: Rhinos and palms in the Miocene
cards.text: The rocks around Red Rock Canyon preserve fossils from the Miocene, between about 13.5 and 7.3 million years ago. They include horses, camels, and three kinds of rhinoceros, along with a shovel-tusker named Serbelodon burnhami. Fossil plants include oak, cypress, and a palm.

cards.title: Where the shuttle came home
cards.text: Edwards Air Force Base, which Highway 14 passes close to at Rosamond, was often one of the main landing strips for NASA's Space Shuttle. On April 14, 1981, the shuttle Columbia touched down on Rogers Dry Lake at Edwards, ending the first shuttle mission after more than two days in space. Astronauts John Young and Robert Crippen were aboard. Crowds of well over 200,000 people watched the landing.

cards.title: Soledad Mountain
cards.text: Soledad Mountain rises just south of Mojave, and gold was first found there in 1894, when prospectors chased the Queen Esther and other veins. In 1933, George Holmes struck the Silver Queen vein, which revived mining across the district and drew in investors from South Africa. The Golden Queen Mining Company was organized in 1935 to consolidate four of the mountain's mines. The mines produced more than 10 million dollars from 1894 to 1942, before a federal wartime order shut down gold mining. By 2016, the mountain had reopened as a modern open-pit, heap-leach mine.

cards.title: The Jawbone Siphon
cards.text: At Jawbone Canyon, the Los Angeles Aqueduct dips into the canyon and back out through a pipe 8,095 feet long, with an 850-foot drop. It is the largest of the pressurized tubes along the aqueduct, and its chief engineer, William Mulholland, called this section the Jawbone Siphon. The pipe uses the pressure developed on the downslope to force the water up the far side. It burst in freezing weather in 1988. Europeans who settled the canyon around 1860 named it Jawbone because its shape resembled a mandible.

cards.title: Named for an animal that is not an antelope
cards.text: The Antelope Valley is named for the pronghorns that roamed there. Pronghorns are not true antelopes, but they have long been mistaken for them because of their close physical similarities with the true antelope of Eurasia. Early settlers, hunters, and travelers recorded many sightings of pronghorns in the valley. Locally caught and butchered pronghorn meat was often sold to local hotels.

cards.title: The western tip of the Mojave
cards.text: The Antelope Valley covers about 2,200 square miles, mostly in northern Los Angeles County and the southeast corner of Kern County. It is bounded by the Garlock and San Andreas fault systems. Joshua trees, California scrub oak, creosote, and wildflowers, notably the California poppy, grow there. People in the valley depend mainly on pumping groundwater from the valley's aquifers and on importing water from the California Aqueduct.

cards.title: The Kiavah Wilderness at the pass
cards.text: Highway 178 crosses Walker Pass at the north boundary of the Kiavah Wilderness. The wilderness was created in 1994 by the California Desert Protection Act, and it takes in the Scodie Mountains. Pinyon pine, juniper, and Joshua trees grow there. The Pacific Crest Trail travels the length of the wilderness for 17 miles.

cards.title: Up Freeman Canyon
cards.text: By 1870, a good wagon road ran the entire distance from Gilroy to Cerro Gordo for travelers using the Walker Pass route. Today Highway 178 serves automobile traffic over the pass, up Freeman Canyon. In the 1870s and 1880s, a hideout of the outlaw Tiburcio Vásquez and Cleovaro Chavez was near the trail at the foot of the pass, on the desert side.

cards.title: The wilderness above the valley
cards.text: Owens Peak Wilderness, in the mountains west of the Indian Wells Valley, was designated by the California Desert Protection Act of 1994. It is a transition zone between the Great Basin, Mojave Desert, and Sierra Nevada ecoregions. Its canyons hold springs with extensive riparian vegetation, with cottonwood and oak trees in the canyons and valleys. The Pacific Crest Trail passes through the wilderness along the crest and western side.

cards.title: Why it's called Poison Canyon
cards.text: Salt Wells Canyon, commonly called Poison Canyon, lies on Highway 178 about 10 miles out of Ridgecrest. It earned the name because the small stream at its west end contains toxic levels of several minerals. Rocks in the canyon known as the Fish Head Rocks were originally called the Whale Heads. They were originally painted sometime in the late 1930s or early 1940s.

cards.title: Trona Road becomes Highway 178
cards.text: About 7.8 miles of Trona Road became part of the state highway system in 1947, with the addition of Legislative Route 212. That portion runs from Poison Canyon westward and is now part of State Route 178. Pinnacle Road, which meets the highway here, is the entrance to the Trona Pinnacles, five miles away.

cards.title: Canebrake Ecological Reserve
cards.text: Canebrake Ecological Reserve lies in the South Fork Valley, on the north side of Highway 178. Before the state acquired it in 1994, the property was a ranch established around 1872. Its habitat types include valley foothill riparian, blue oak and digger pine, and Joshua tree. Hundreds of bird species occur there, and the cottonwood-willow forest shelters the endangered southwestern willow flycatcher and the state-listed western yellow-billed cuckoo.

cards.title: Where the Pacific Crest Trail meets the highway
cards.text: Walker Pass Campground sits just off Highway 178, at the junction of the Owens Peak and Cache Peak segments of the Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail. It has eleven walk-in sites for Pacific Crest Trail hikers and tent campers, plus two sites for car camping. Pinyon pines and a few Joshua trees grow there, but no drinking water is available at the site.

cards.title: When this was Route 6
cards.text: From 1937 until 1964, this road was part of US Route 6, which had been extended from Greeley, Colorado, to Long Beach, California, on June 21, 1937. South of Inyokern, US 6 continued on to Long Beach. On July 1, 1964, US 6 was truncated at Bishop, and the part from Inyokern to Los Angeles became State Route 14.

cards.title: The Garlock Fault
cards.text: Johannesburg is one of the communities closest to the Garlock Fault, which is about 250 kilometers, or 160 miles, long. The two sides of the fault slide past each other horizontally, in what geologists call left-lateral motion. The last significant surface ruptures are thought to have come about 1050 A.D. near Tehachapi and about 1500 A.D. near Johannesburg. No earthquake has produced surface rupture on the Garlock Fault in historic times, though a magnitude 5.7 earthquake occurred in 1992. The fault is named for the mining town of Garlock, founded in 1894 by Eugene Garlock and now a ghost town.

cards.title: A test track in the desert
cards.text: The Honda Proving Center of California, near Cantil, has a 7.5-mile oval track and a 5-mile winding road course. It was established in 1990 and used mainly to test Honda and Acura automobiles, though motorcycles are tested there too. Honda closed it in 2010 and moved testing to Marysville, Ohio, then announced in 2015 that it would renovate and expand it. The renovated center opened in May 2017.

cards.title: A stone cliff on the railroad
cards.text: Cantil is Spanish for stone cliff, and it was one of a series of C names chosen for this stretch of railroad, along with Cambio, Cinco, and Ceneda. It was founded as a station on the Nevada and California Railroad in 1908 or 1909, when the line was extended from Owens Lake to Mojave. The first post office opened in 1916.

cards.title: The day SpaceShipTwo broke apart
cards.text: On October 31, 2014, Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo crashed in the Mojave Desert near Cantil, killing one of its two pilots. The craft broke apart during its fourth rocket-powered test flight, and debris was strewn across a 5-mile track near Koehn Lake. The surviving pilot, Peter Siebold, was badly hurt but lived, because his seat was ejected as the craft broke apart and he used a parachute. Investigators found that the copilot, Michael Alsbury, unlocked the tail feathering system too early, at Mach 0.8 instead of Mach 1.4.

cards.title: The Acres
cards.text: China Lake Acres, which local residents call The Acres, had 1,757 people at the 2020 census. That was down from 1,876 in 2010. It first appeared as a census-designated place in the 2000 census. It covers about 5.2 square miles, nearly all of it land.

cards.title: Coyote Holes
cards.text: Freeman Junction began as a stagecoach stop run by Freeman S. Raymond, a forty-niner, at a place called Coyote Holes. The place had that name because coyotes visited the springs there in droves to quench their thirst. The station stood where the Walker Pass road, now California 178, met the road to Los Angeles, now California 14. Raymond kept the stop going, with a post office added after 1889 or 1890, until his death in August 1909.

cards.title: A junction of old trails
cards.text: A bedrock mortar site near the original spring suggests that Native Americans regularly camped at what is now Freeman Junction. Explorer Joseph R. Walker passed this junction of Indian trails in 1834, and forty-niner parties split here after escaping Death Valley, some going west and some south. California registered the site as a historical landmark in 1961. By 1978 the town had died and its remains were removed by passersby, and today nothing remains.

cards.title: The bandit at Coyote Holes
cards.text: On February 25, 1874, the outlaw Tiburcio Vásquez and his band robbed several freight wagon crews at Freeman Raymond's station, which was then called Coyote Holes. Vásquez preyed on stages and freighters traveling between the Kern River mines and Los Angeles.

cards.title: A runway for car commercials
cards.text: Inyokern Airport's long runways, a legacy of the Navy's wartime buildup, have made it a popular place to film car commercials. Ads shot there include most spots from Saab's Born from Jets campaign, as well as ads for Volkswagen and Volvo. Top Gun: Maverick used the airport's hangar for scenes of Tom Cruise working on a vintage aircraft.

cards.title: Harvey Field
cards.text: Inyokern's airfield was dedicated as Harvey Field on May 10, 1944, in honor of Navy Lieutenant Commander Warren Harvey, for his work on aviation ordnance and fighter tactics. The Navy closed Harvey Field in April 1946 and returned it to the county a year later.

cards.title: A railroad town on the county line
cards.text: Inyokern takes its name from its location near the border between Inyo and Kern Counties. It was a railroad town, established along the Southern Pacific's Lone Pine Branch, which has since been removed. That branch ran north from Mojave to Owenyo, a few miles north of Lone Pine, and was built around 1912 and used to help build the Los Angeles Aqueduct. Inyokern's first post office opened in 1910. The 2020 census counted 988 people, down from 1,099 in 2010.

cards.title: The desert video
cards.text: Alice in Chains filmed the music video for Down in a Hole in Johannesburg on August 9, 1993. Nigel Dick directed it, and the storyline shows the band members walking through a desert landscape. The video premiered in September 1993.

cards.title: Named by miners from South Africa
cards.text: Johannesburg was named by miners who had previously worked in the gold-producing region of South Africa. It was founded as a supply town for the mines at Randsburg, and the first post office opened in 1897. Locals and frequent visitors often call it Joburg.

cards.title: A town of about a hundred
cards.text: Johannesburg had 113 people at the 2020 census, down from 172 at the 2010 census. That is a drop of about a third in ten years.

cards.title: The railway to the mines
cards.text: The Randsburg Railway ran 28.5 miles from Kramer Junction, on the Santa Fe main line, to Johannesburg, with a stop at Atolia. It opened in January 1898 as a supply link to the Rand Mine. The Santa Fe bought the railway in 1903. It ceased operations on December 30, 1933, a victim of the Great Depression and a decline in the mining industry.

cards.title: The state fish of the Kern
cards.text: The golden trout has been California's official freshwater state fish since 1947. California golden trout are native to two stream systems on the eastern side of the Kern River: Golden Trout Creek and the South Fork Kern River. The fish was named for Agua Bonita Waterfall, where the first specimens were collected. In 1876, 13 golden trout were put in a coffee can and carried to Cottonwood Creek.

cards.title: Lake Isabella by the numbers
cards.text: Lake Isabella had 3,573 people at the 2020 census, up from 3,466 at the 2010 census. It sits where the North and South Forks of the Kern River meet.

cards.title: A town named in 1893
cards.text: The town of Isabella was founded by Steven Barton in 1893 and named in honor of Queen Isabella of Spain. Her name was popular during the 1893 Columbian Exposition.

cards.title: A town that moved and changed its name
cards.text: When the Isabella dam created the lake in 1953, the town of Isabella had to move about 1.5 miles south of its original site. Its post office operated at the original site from 1896 to 1953, then at the new site until the name was changed to Lake Isabella in 1957. The original site was inundated by the lake.

cards.title: Where the name Lancaster came from
cards.text: Nobody is sure where Lancaster got its name. It has been attributed to the surname of a railroad station clerk, to a nickname given by railroad officials, or to Lancaster, Pennsylvania, the former home of unknown settlers. The settlement began with the Southern Pacific Railroad, which completed its line through the Antelope Valley in 1876, linking San Francisco and Los Angeles.

cards.title: When the poppies bloom
cards.text: The California poppies at the Antelope Valley poppy reserve usually bloom from mid-February through mid-May. How well they bloom depends on how much rain falls in winter and early spring. State parks does not water or stimulate the flowers, to keep the fields in a strictly natural state.

cards.title: Pennies for Poppies
cards.text: The Antelope Valley California Poppy Reserve, west of Lancaster, grew out of the work of a self-taught artist named Jane S. Pinheiro, who recognized that rapid development threatened the poppy fields. Schoolchildren across California helped by collecting Pennies for Poppies. The reserve was established in 1976. It protects about 1,800 acres.

cards.title: How many people live in Lancaster
cards.text: Lancaster had 173,516 people at the 2020 census. It lies in the Antelope Valley of the western Mojave Desert, about 70 miles north of downtown Los Angeles.

cards.title: The first city to require solar roofs
cards.text: In March 2013, the Lancaster city council voted unanimously to require solar panels on new homes, making it the first city in the United States to do so. The rule took effect on January 1, 2014. Homes on lots of 7,000 square feet or more must have a solar system of 1.0 to 1.5 kilowatts.

cards.title: Rebuilding the main street in eight months
cards.text: Lancaster rebuilt a stretch of its main street, Lancaster Boulevard, as The BLVD, finished in 2010. Construction took eight months and cost 11.5 million dollars. A 30-foot-wide shaded central walkway, called a ramblas, was inspired by a thoroughfare in Barcelona. The project created more than 800 permanent jobs, along with 1,100 temporary construction jobs.

cards.title: The Aerospace Walk of Honor
cards.text: Lancaster's Aerospace Walk of Honor was established in 1990 to honor test pilots who flew at Edwards Air Force Base. Its first honorees in 1990 included Chuck Yeager and James H. Doolittle, and Neil Armstrong followed in 1991. The program was completed in 2009, when the 100th honoree was inducted. Sidewalk monuments along Lancaster Boulevard still honor the pilots.

cards.title: Hotels and Harvey Girls
cards.text: Mojave's hospitality trade began with the opening of the Morrissey Hotel in 1876. The Fred Harvey organization also operated a Harvey House there, with Harvey Girls serving meals.

cards.title: A name from the Colorado River
cards.text: Mojave takes its name from the Mohave Indian nation, whose homeland was on the Colorado River. The word Mojave is Spanish for Hamakhava, the name of that nation.

cards.title: Mojave by the numbers
cards.text: About 4,700 people lived in Mojave at the 2020 census, up from 4,238 in 2010. The 2000 census counted 3,836. Mojave is 50 miles southeast of Bakersfield and 100 miles north of Los Angeles.

cards.title: A town laid out by the railroad
cards.text: During World War II, several local women in Mojave worked for the Southern Pacific maintaining locomotives in the railroad's roundhouse. The railroad established a yard in Mojave and made it a division point. The railroad also laid out the town, and its layout and street names were still in use after 135 years. Wind turbine components now move from rail cars to trucks at the Mojave Air and Space Port.

cards.title: The longest wingspan ever flown
cards.text: The Stratolaunch Roc, which has the longest wingspan ever flown at 385 feet, first flew from Mojave Air and Space Port on April 13, 2019. Its twin fuselages are each 238 feet long, and it is powered by six Pratt and Whitney engines. About half of its empty weight comes from parts of a Boeing 747-400. It was designed to carry rockets aloft for launch into orbit, and it has since carried a hypersonic test vehicle.

cards.title: Mountain Mesa by the numbers
cards.text: Mountain Mesa had 823 people at the 2020 census, up from 777 at the 2010 census. It first appeared as a census-designated place in the 1990 census, when it counted 1,153 people. By 2000 that count had fallen to 716. The community covers less than one square mile, about 0.87 square miles, all of it land.

cards.title: Land returned to the Tübatulabal
cards.text: The Tübatulabal Tribe acquired about 1,240 acres of its ancestral land in a 5 million dollar purchase. The state Wildlife Conservation Board and the Sierra Nevada Conservancy funded the purchase, and another 1,000 acres were deeded to the Kern County Heritage Foundation. The tribe plans an office, a cultural center, and public hiking trails, and it plans to invite schools to learn there. The tribe has 280 enrolled members, and as a political entity it is not federally recognized.

cards.title: A state off-road area on the old ranch
cards.text: The Eastern Kern County Onyx Ranch State Vehicular Recreation Area became a state off-highway vehicle area in 2014. It covers about 25,000 acres, and it offers riding for motorcycles, all-terrain vehicles, and four-wheel-drive vehicles. Visitors also use it for rock hounding, bird and wildlife viewing, and hunting. It is about 0.5 percent of Kern County, as of 2024.

cards.title: From Scodie to Onyx
cards.text: Onyx was originally called Scodie, for William Scodie, who opened a store there in 1861. The first post office at Onyx opened in 1889. The community sits in the South Fork Valley. The 2020 census counted 457 people, down from 475 in 2010.

cards.title: A boom town of thousands
cards.text: By 1900, roughly 3,500 to 4,000 people lived in Randsburg. The town had a 30-stamp ore crusher, a bank, churches, and theaters. At the turn of the century, when gold was worth only 12 to 16 dollars an ounce, the Yellow Aster Mine recovered 3 million dollars in gold. Two fires within months of each other destroyed much of the town, and a third took out most of the remaining buildings.

cards.title: A living ghost town
cards.text: Randsburg is called a living ghost town, and on weekends motorcyclists and tourists stop in to explore the old buildings and visit the general store. Most visitors arrive between autumn and spring because of the extreme heat in summer. Thanksgiving weekend and New Year's Eve are exceptions, when tourists flock into the town.

cards.title: Randsburg on screen
cards.text: The lost 1913 movie The Mystery of Yellow Aster Mine was shot in Randsburg. South of Suez, starring George Brent and released in November 1940, was filmed there. Dwight Yoakam's 1989 video for Long White Cadillac was filmed in Randsburg too. Scenes from the 2011 film Cowboys and Aliens were also filmed in the town.

cards.title: Water trucked in
cards.text: In Red Mountain, locals truck in water to avoid the arsenic that decades of mining left in the ground and in their tap water. Soil testing has found as much as 10,000 milligrams of arsenic per kilogram in some parts of the community. In 2022, Red Mountain received a 1.5 million dollar grant to clean arsenic-laden sediment left by historic gold and silver mining at the Kelly mine complex.

cards.title: The California Rand Silver Mine
cards.text: In June 1919, Williams and Nosser discovered the California Rand Silver Mine at Red Mountain. From June 1919 to August 1923, the mine produced over 7 million dollars. By 1926 its total gross production was over 13 million dollars, with dividends totaling 4.5 million. In 1929 the mine could not be operated profitably, and it was sold for 50,000 dollars.

cards.title: Born as Osdick
cards.text: Red Mountain was established in 1919 as Osdick, a silver mine boom town. It was named for a miner named Osdick who held claims there. The post office opened under the name Osdick in 1922 and was later renamed Red Mountain.

cards.title: What the silver left behind
cards.text: When the silver market took a nosedive, Red Mountain's good fortune went with it, and people drifted away. Old headframes and dusty relics can still be seen along the road. The 2010 census counted 131 people in Red Mountain.

cards.title: Before the town
cards.text: The Paiute, Shoshone, and Kawaiisu peoples all lived in the Indian Wells Valley long before Ridgecrest existed. Permanent non-Native communities did not form until the early 1900s, when the Los Angeles Aqueduct and the Southern Pacific Railroad helped spark farming settlements.

cards.title: A town ringed by four ranges
cards.text: Ridgecrest is surrounded by four mountain ranges: the Sierra Nevada to the west, the Coso Range to the north, the Argus Range to the east, and the El Paso Mountains to the south. It sits in the Indian Wells Valley, in northeastern Kern County, next to the Navy's China Lake base.

cards.title: From dairy settlement to city
cards.text: Ridgecrest grew to more than 5,000 people by the 1950s, after the Naval Ordnance Test Station was set up at Harvey Field in 1943. It incorporated as a city in 1963. The 2020 census counted 27,959 people.

cards.title: Holes in the desert
cards.text: The 2003 film Holes was shot in several locations, including Ridgecrest. Because of the constant heat, the cast was allowed to stay in the holes for only about five minutes at a time, and would be pulled out even in the middle of a take.

cards.title: A Blink-182 founder from Ridgecrest
cards.text: Mark Hoppus, bassist and singer of the rock band Blink-182, was born in Ridgecrest on March 15, 1972. He left in the summer of 1992 for San Diego, to attend college and work at a local music store. That August, he and Tom DeLonge were introduced and began playing music in DeLonge's garage.

cards.title: The Maturango Museum
cards.text: The Maturango Museum in Ridgecrest was founded in 1962 to highlight the history of Ridgecrest and nearby China Lake. It is best known for guided tours of the Coso Rock Art District on the China Lake base, but because of restrictions from the base command, those tours were not available to the public when last reported. The museum is also an archaeological repository for qualified individuals, taking in artifacts from the Sierra Nevada to Death Valley.

cards.title: Crumville, and a one-vote name
cards.text: Ridgecrest began in 1912 as a farming community called Crumville, named for two local dairymen, James and Robert Crum. In 1941, the community wanted a new name, but postal authorities rejected its first choice, Sierra View, because there were already too many Sierras. Ada Thompson suggested Ridgecrest, and it won by a single vote over the name Gilmore. The first post office opened that same year.

cards.title: A railroad official's daughter
cards.text: Rosamond got its name from a Southern Pacific Railroad official who named the town after his daughter. The rails reached Rosamond in 1876, as they did in Tehachapi and Mojave. Rosamond was established in 1877 as a townsite owned by the Southern Pacific Railroad. During the 1890s, gold was discovered in the area, quickly drawing miners and prospectors. The 2020 census counted 20,961 people.

cards.title: Gold in the fire clay
cards.text: Ezra Hamilton owned a pottery in Los Angeles and made bricks and pipe from fire clay mined at Tropico Hill, near Willow Springs. In the 1890s he found gold in that clay, and a gold mine followed. The Tropico mill, built in the 1920s with a rotary ball mill circuit, was part of operations that generated about 50,000 tons of tailings. Glenn and Doreen Settle later turned the property into a Gold Camp, where a World Champion Gold Panning Contest was held each year.

cards.title: The Fastest Road in the West
cards.text: Construction of Willow Springs Raceway began in 1952, and the first race was held on November 23, 1953. The surface started out as oiled dirt and was paved by 1954. The 2.5-mile main track still has its original layout, and it earned the nickname The Fastest Road in the West. In 1996, California declared the raceway a Point of Historical Interest.

cards.title: A company town for potash
cards.text: In 1913, the British-owned Consolidated Gold Fields of South Africa founded the American Trona Corporation, which set up Trona as a company-run town. In 1914, the Trona Railway opened a 31-mile line from Trona to the Southern Pacific junction at Searles Station. The railway was built to bring the company's potash to an interchange with the Southern Pacific. A heavily financed refinery at Trona was completed in October 1916.

cards.title: The Pinnacles on screen
cards.text: Films shot at the Trona Pinnacles include Star Trek V: The Final Frontier, Lost in Space, and Planet of the Apes. Rihanna's 2016 video for Sledgehammer was also shot there.

cards.title: A lake of chemicals
cards.text: John Searles discovered borax on the surface of Searles Lake in 1862. Plants at Argus, Trona, and Westend still extract industrial minerals from the lake's brines. The products include borax, boric acid, soda ash, and salt. The dry lake basin is about 12 miles long and about 8 miles wide at its widest point.

cards.title: The Pit
cards.text: Trona High School plays football on a field of dirt and sand called The Pit, because the salt in the soil kills grass. The school's teams are the Tornadoes, but the football players call themselves the Sandmen.

cards.title: Five hundred stone spires
cards.text: The Trona Pinnacles are more than 500 tufa spires, some as high as 140 feet, rising from the bed of the Searles Lake basin. They formed underwater between 10,000 and 100,000 years ago, when Searles Lake was a link in a chain of interconnected lakes. The area was once under 640 feet of water, during the Pleistocene. A 5-mile dirt road leads to them, usually passable in a two-wheel-drive vehicle, though it may be closed after heavy rain.

cards.title: Where the name Trona comes from
cards.text: The name Trona is derived from the mineral trona, which is abundant in Searles Lake. Searles Valley includes the unincorporated communities of Argus, Pioneer Point, Searles Valley, and Trona. The 2020 census counted 1,565 people.

cards.title: Camp Leonard, 1863
cards.text: Camp Leonard was established at Weldon in the late summer of 1863 by a company of the 2nd California Volunteer Cavalry, to protect the region's mining camps. Some 850 Native people from the Owens Valley had left the Sebastian Indian Reservation because of the scarcity of food there, all intent on returning to their former homes. The camp stayed in operation for the rest of that year.

cards.title: A cattle rancher's name
cards.text: Weldon is named for William B. Weldon, a cattle rancher. The Weldon post office opened in 1871. The town sits at the southeast tip of Lake Isabella.

cards.title: Weldon by the numbers
cards.text: Weldon had 2,303 people at the 2020 census, down from 2,642 at the 2010 census. The count fell by about 340 people in ten years.

cards.title: The Inter-Tribal Ceremonial
cards.text: The Gallup Inter-Tribal Indian Ceremonial was first held in 1922, started by traders who wanted to bring in tourists and showcase local tribes. It now runs for about ten days around the start of August at Red Rock Park. Parades through downtown Gallup show off the variety of tribes taking part, alongside a rodeo and a Native arts marketplace. The 2026 gathering was the 104th.

cards.title: A corner of Chaco
cards.text: By the year 1050, Chaco Canyon was the ceremonial, administrative, and economic center of the San Juan Basin, and a small corner of the park that protects it lies in McKinley County. The Chacoan people's cultural flowering began in the mid 800s and lasted more than 300 years. Chaco is also central to the origins of several Navajo clans.

cards.title: The checkerboard
cards.text: Close to a fifth of McKinley County is Navajo Nation off-reservation trust land, as of 2024. Across the eastern Navajo region, land became a checkerboard, with Navajo allotments and tribal trust land scattered among private, railroad, and state holdings. The Eastern Navajo Agency checkerboard is distinct from the rest of the reservation, even in which federal programs control it.

cards.title: After the Church Rock spill
cards.text: After the Church Rock uranium spill, the Navajo Nation asked New Mexico's governor to declare a state of emergency and to seek a federal disaster declaration. The governor said no. A warning sign posted along the Puerco River after the spill told residents, in English, Spanish, and Diné, to stay away from the water. The mill was allowed to start up again within months of the spill, and in 1983 the site was put on the national Superfund priority list.

cards.title: The Church Rock spill
cards.text: Before dawn on July 16, 1979, the dam holding back a tailings pond at the Church Rock uranium mill gave way. About a thousand tons of radioactive mill waste and more than 90 million gallons of acidic, radioactive liquid poured out. The flood ran down Pipeline Arroyo into the Puerco River. Contamination traveled about 80 miles downstream, into Navajo County, Arizona.

cards.title: Warm days, cold nights
cards.text: In Gallup, July afternoons average close to 89 degrees, but January nights average about 14. The year brings only about 11 inches of rain and melted snow. Even so, about 34 inches of snow falls in a typical year. Averaged over the whole year, the temperature comes to about 50 degrees.

cards.title: The Gallup coal field
cards.text: Coal mining around Gallup began in the early 1880s, when the railroad was built through the area. The first mine opened in 1882, and underground mining went on until the 1950s. Big surface mines took over in the 1960s, and by 2008 the Gallup area had produced more than 218 million tons of coal. The area's major strip mine, the McKinley Mine, ran for 47 years.

cards.title: Fires underground
cards.text: In the summer of 2024, state crews dug out and put out two underground coal-mine fires just outside Gallup. One was burning within 100 feet of the new Navajo-Gallup Water Supply pipeline, which carries water for about 250,000 people. When the burning seams were exposed, temperatures shot to 550 degrees within minutes. Old mine workings also lie beneath Gallup itself, under housing tracts, schools, and shopping centers.

cards.title: The 1933 coal strike
cards.text: On August 29, 1933, coal miners around Gallup walked off the job. They were angry over wage cuts and low pay for so-called deadwork, and the coal company's general manager told their union the answer was no. The governor declared martial law, and National Guard troops held the town for months.

cards.title: Sworn in at Fort Wingate
cards.text: The first 29 Navajo Code Talkers were sworn into the Marine Corps at Fort Wingate, in McKinley County, on May 4, 1942. Fort Wingate sits about 15 miles east-southeast of Gallup. Nearly 400 Navajo Marines went on to serve as code talkers across the Pacific. In 2001, Congress awarded each of those first 29 recruits the Congressional Gold Medal.

cards.title: Crossing the Continental Divide
cards.text: In central McKinley County, Interstate 40 crosses the Continental Divide at Campbell Pass, 7,275 feet up. Signs in the median mark the spot, and state historic markers stand on the service roads on each side. Starting in 1926, this pass also carried Route 66, and remnants of the old roadside are still around. A small community called Continental Divide sits at the pass, about 25 miles east-southeast of Gallup.

cards.title: Running the county
cards.text: McKinley County's government had about 220 full-time employees in 2022, and no part-time staff. That year it spent about 54 million dollars. It collected about 24 million dollars in taxes, about 17 million of it from property taxes and about 7 million from gross receipts and sales taxes.

cards.title: Climbing toward the Divide
cards.text: Interstate 40 climbs about a thousand feet as it crosses McKinley County from the Arizona line. Near the state line, the road sits at roughly 6,200 feet. At the Continental Divide at Campbell Pass, it reaches 7,275 feet.

cards.title: Fort Wingate
cards.text: Redstone and Pershing missiles were tested in the 1960s at Fort Wingate, about 15 miles east-southeast of Gallup. An army post was set up at its site, Bear Springs, in 1860, and Fort Wingate moved there in 1868. Navajo people returning from Bosque Redondo were settled there for a time. It remained a major weapons depot until it closed in 1993. Its land is now being returned to the Navajo and Zuni.

cards.title: The 1935 Gallup riot
cards.text: On April 4, 1935, gunfire broke out in Gallup as a crowd gathered to free men arrested in a fight over evictions of miners' families. The county sheriff and two others died. In the crackdown that followed, special deputies made sweeping arrests, and Mexican citizens were deported. Three men were convicted of second-degree murder; one conviction was overturned, and the other two were pardoned in 1939.

cards.title: Who holds the land
cards.text: More than half of McKinley County is tribal land, as of 2024. Navajo Nation lands cover more than two fifths of the county, and the Zuni Reservation nearly a tenth. The Bureau of Land Management manages about 7 percent, the Cibola National Forest about 6, and state trust land about 5.

cards.title: Languages at home
cards.text: About half of McKinley County residents speak a language other than English at home, as of 2024, and Spanish accounts for only about 3,000 of them. One of the languages heard here is Zuni, a language isolate with no known relatives. It is spoken mostly around Zuni Pueblo. Its speakers call it Shiwi'ma.

cards.title: A county named for a president
cards.text: McKinley County is named for President William McKinley. New Mexico's territorial legislature passed the act creating it on February 23, 1899, carving it out of Bernalillo County. The law took effect, and the county came into being, on January 1, 1901. Its county seat is Gallup.

cards.title: Diné Bikéyah
cards.text: More than two fifths of McKinley County is Navajo Nation land, as of 2024. About a quarter of the county is Navajo reservation, and close to a fifth more is off-reservation trust land. Diné Bikéyah, or Navajoland, reaches into Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico, covering over 27,000 square miles.

cards.title: Who lives here
cards.text: About 70,000 people live in McKinley County, as of 2024, spread across about 5,450 square miles of land. Half of its residents are younger than about 35. The median household income was about 47,700 dollars a year. The median home was worth about 79,000 dollars.

cards.title: Rails, Route 66, and the interstate
cards.text: In 1880, the railroad chose a low pass over the Continental Divide in McKinley County for its line from Albuquerque to Southern California. Gallup was founded the next year, in 1881. That line is still one of the BNSF Railway's main transcontinental routes, and Interstate 40 runs alongside it through Gallup. The interstate replaced Route 66, and its bypass around Gallup was finished in 1980.

cards.title: The uranium boom
cards.text: In 1950, a Navajo sheepherder named Paddy Martinez found uranium at Haystack, near Grants. The find was on Santa Fe Railroad land, and the railroad paid him 250 dollars a month for the rest of his life. The Grants uranium district stretches from east of Laguna to west of Gallup, and most of New Mexico's uranium came from its deposits in McKinley and Cibola Counties. From 1951 to 1980, it yielded more uranium than any other district in the United States.

cards.title: Uranium around Church Rock and Crownpoint
cards.text: The western edge of the Grants uranium district, around Church Rock and Crownpoint in McKinley County, is also known as the Gallup subdistrict. It holds more than 50 known uranium occurrences, and its mines produced more than 16 million pounds of uranium oxide between 1952 and 1986. Contamination there, and in the Smith Lake and Nose Rock areas, falls partly under the Navajo Nation's jurisdiction and is being addressed by the federal Environmental Protection Agency. Across the district, open shafts and uncontrolled piles of waste rock remain at many old mine sites.

cards.title: Hollywood westerns
cards.text: In the 1940s and 1950s, Hollywood crews came to the rugged country around Gallup to shoot westerns on location. Films made there include Pursued, Four Faces West, and Escape from Fort Bravo. Crews and stars used Gallup's El Rancho Hotel as their base, encouraged by its owner, R. E. Griffith, and his brother, the director D. W. Griffith. By 1964, the lure of the western hero was fading.

cards.title: The Middle Place
cards.text: The Zuni people call themselves A:shiwi, and in Zuni tradition their ancestors searched for ages for Halona:wa Idiwan'a, the Middle Place. About a tenth of McKinley County is the Zuni Reservation, as of 2024. Almost everyone on the reservation lives in Zuni Pueblo, about 40 miles south of Gallup, or in nearby Black Rock. Photography permits are available, but photography is not allowed at ceremonies.
